narrative: The model estimated a 72% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admission decision treated that estimate as a serious academic-risk signal, your law school application was rejected. The strongest reason was your third-year class standing: you were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That gap was the single largest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.30 was slightly above the accepted-student average of 3.23, so it worked in your favor and pushed toward passing, but it was only the second-most influential factor and could not offset the concern about later academic performance. Your upper-middle family-income background was the third-most influential factor and also modestly pushed toward passing; it is common among accepted students, so it did not create the rejection risk. Overall, the model saw strength in your GPA and background, but the low third-year standing dominated. To improve future chances, focus on evidence that your later academic performance is stronger: consider additional coursework or credentials, prepare to retake the standardized test if permitted, and seek advising on programs that review context holistically. You may also ask an admissions adviser how to explain any circumstances behind your third-year ranking.
